security_audit.summary: The static results are false positives caused by Markdown syntax, documented private-network examples, and constrained local file or command handling. Two high-severity design risks remain: TLS peer verification is disabled by default, and printer access codes are written to plaintext configuration without restrictive permissions. No prompt injection, obfuscation, or malicious data-exfiltration intent was found.

remediation.issue: TLS connections do not authenticate the printer by default.
remediation.suggestion: Pin each printer certificate or fingerprint during trusted onboarding, reject changes, and require an explicit warning-confirmed override for unauthenticated TLS.

remediation.issue: Printer access codes are stored in a regular plaintext JSON file.
remediation.suggestion: Use an operating-system secret store when available and create fallback configuration atomically with owner-only 0600 permissions.

remediation.issue: Repository exclusion for the credential file is advisory only.
remediation.suggestion: Verify bambu-printers.json is ignored before writing credentials and warn when the workspace is not protected from version-control inclusion.

semantic_findings.title: Printer TLS Authentication Disabled by Default
semantic_findings.description: FTPS, MQTT, and serial-discovery connections disable certificate verification unless users opt in. A local network attacker could impersonate the printer, capture its access code, or alter control traffic.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The code explicitly sets CERT_NONE and disables hostname checks before authenticating with the printer access code. This behavior occurs on every main TLS workflow by default.

semantic_findings.title: Printer Access Code Stored Without Restricted Permissions
semantic_findings.description: The configuration writer stores the printer access code as plaintext using default file permissions. Other local users or accidental repository inclusion could expose a credential that permits printer control.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The access code is assigned directly into the JSON object and write_text creates the file under the process umask. No chmod, secure secret store, or enforced ignore rule protects it.

content.user_title: Manage Bambu Lab LAN Print Jobs Safely
content.value_statement: Local Bambu print handoffs require careful file validation, device setup, and physical safeguards. This skill plans, uploads, starts, pauses, and cancels jobs through local FTPS and MQTT.
actual_capabilities: Inspects plain G-code files and reports file size and MD5 before handoff.
Creates dry-run plans before upload, start, pause, cancel, or error-clear requests.
Uploads plain G-code or packaged project files to a configured printer through implicit FTPS.
Publishes start and control requests through the printer local MQTT interface.
Reads printer status reports and annotates available HMS error codes.
Packages supported jobs with bambox or a known compatible project template.
limitations: It does not create models, slice geometry, or validate print quality.
Local printing depends on undocumented printer behavior that can change with firmware.
Bambox packaging supports only enabled printer, nozzle, and filament profiles.
TLS certificates are not verified by default, so use only a trusted local network.

use_cases.title: Prepare a First LAN Handoff
use_cases.description: Configure one printer, verify status, and review a dry-run upload plan without starting a print.

use_cases.title: Upload a Validated Workshop Job
use_cases.description: Inspect and upload approved G-code to a known printer before a supervised start.

use_cases.title: Diagnose Local Print Control
use_cases.description: Collect MQTT status, inspect acknowledgements, and compare supported handoff modes during integration testing.

prompt_templates.title: Check Printer Setup
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me configure my [printer model] for local LAN use. Stop after status verification and do not upload or start a print.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new printer

prompt_templates.title: Review a Dry-Run Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Inspect [G-code path] for printer [printer id] and show the safest dry-run handoff plan. Do not execute network actions.
prompt_templates.scenario: Validate a prepared job before upload

prompt_templates.title: Upload Without Starting
prompt_templates.prompt: Upload [G-code path] to [printer id] using [handoff mode]. Verify printer status first, execute upload only, and report the result.
prompt_templates.scenario: Stage a job for later supervised printing

prompt_templates.title: Run a Supervised Project Handoff
prompt_templates.prompt: For [printer id], validate [G-code path], inspect status, package with [template or bambox profile], upload, and start only when every safety check passes.

output_examples.input: Check whether my configured A1 Mini is ready for a local print.
output_examples.output: The printer responded and is idle. Storage is available, no active HMS issue was reported, and no file was uploaded.

output_examples.input: Prepare an upload plan for my validated enclosure G-code.
output_examples.output: Dry-run complete. The plan identifies the local file, remote project name, FTPS destination, MQTT topic, and required start confirmation.

output_examples.input: Pause the active print and confirm the result.
output_examples.output: The pause request was published to the configured printer. A follow-up status report indicates the job is paused.

best_practices: Use a trusted local network and verify the configured printer identity before live actions.
Review dry-run output, upload first, then start only with a clear user request and physical supervision.
Keep access codes outside version control and restrict credential-file permissions to the current user.
anti_patterns: Do not start a print from unvalidated G-code or an incompatible project template.
Do not bypass private-host checks or disable safeguards to reach an internet-hosted endpoint.
Do not treat an MQTT publish acknowledgement as proof that printing started safely.

faq.question: Does this skill slice STL or CAD files?
faq.answer: No. It requires an existing validated plain G-code file and handles the local printer handoff.

faq.question: Can it start a print automatically?
faq.answer: A live start requires execution mode and an explicit start-confirmation flag after validation and status checks.

faq.question: Which network protocols does it use?
faq.answer: It uses implicit FTPS for file upload and MQTT over TLS for status and printer controls.

faq.question: Where is printer configuration stored?
faq.answer: The default is bambu-printers.json in the workspace root. It can contain a sensitive LAN access code.

faq.question: Which project handoff mode should I use?
faq.answer: Use a validated same-printer template where documented. Use plain mode only on verified firmware and bambox only for enabled profiles.

faq.question: Does it confirm that a print is physically safe?
faq.answer: No. The operator must verify the build plate, material, nozzle, surroundings, and first-layer behavior at the printer.
